newsitem.title: UK: Clashes in Germany mar European mayday parades.
newsitem.headline: Clashes in Germany mar European mayday parades.

text.p: Violent clashes in Germany on Thursday marred European workers' traditional May Day parades.
Hundreds of neo-Nazis and dozens of left-wing extremists smashed windows and rampaged through the northern town of Muenden after police broke up an illegal right-wing rally.
In Liepzig, around 150 left-wingers hurled rocks and fireworks at police, who were trying to keep them apart from a small group of skinheads.
Police in Berlin, too, were bracing for trouble.
Demonstrators there have targeted expensive cars, shops and bars in the past. They went on the rampage 10 years ago on May 1, setting fire to a supermarket.
The annual workers' celebration -- given extra bite this year by soaring unemployment in Europe -- offered a good chance to bring politics on to the streets in other cities too.
In Paris, far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and his National Front launched their drive for a foothold in parliament by marching through the heart of the capital.
Le Pen's annual May Day festival, honouring French mediaeval heroine Joan of Arc, was broadened this year to vaunt Front hopes of winning seats in the National Assembly, where it currently has none.
Some 5,000 party loyalists turned out for the demonstration in bright sunshine as,across the city, leftist trade unions planned a labour march later in the day.
In Russia, the festivities were helped along by liberal amounts of vodka.
Outside the Kremlin walls, police estimated a turnout of about 25,000 communist supporters carrying red flags and slogans demanding President Boris Yeltsin's removal.
"All workers should say 'Boris, go away,'" said Viktor Anpilov, head of the hardline communist Working Russia movement.

Later the crowd, estimated at 100,000 by organisers, approved a resolution "demanding the firing of President Yeltsin who has committed monstrous crimes against the country and the people which is inexcusable".
At a tamer union-sponsored march of a few thousand people outside Moscow's City Hall, the mood was more festive.
Musicians and dancers in traditional dress performed under hazy sun on one of the first warm days at the end of the long Russian winter.
In Kazakhstan, several hundred elderly demonstrators, nostalgic for the Soviet past, gathered in a park amid red flags and bunting in the capital Almaty to protest over unpaid pensions and wages.
One banner trumpeted the traditional Soviet call "Proletarians of all countries -- unite!" while another, more prosaic placard declared: "Capitalism is shit."
Bunches of red carnations were placed at the foot of a statue of Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin, which was quietly removed by the authorities from the city centre last year.
Politics were also centre stage in Britain, as the country voted in a general election likely to result in a win for the traditionally worker-friendly Labour Party.
But in the villages, May Day celebrations were driven mainly by rural tradition.
Long before people cast votes, they celebrated nature and welcomed the coming of spring with traditional songs and dances round the May Pole.
Outside Europe, China chose May Day to warn its workers that economic reform could cost their jobs.

"With reform becoming an irreversible trend in socialist China, the working class, as the masters of the country, are leading the trend as the main force in, as well as a strong driving force for, reform," said a front-page editorial in the People's Daily.
Labour Day is one of the few national holidays in China, whose constitution enshrines the dictatorship of the proletariat.
